title: AI Writing Detectors: What to Do When Your Work Gets Flagged
body_md:
Bottom line: An AI-writing score is a reason to review a document, not proof that its author cheated. If you are a student, a freelancer or a manager, the useful next step is to preserve the writing process and check the applicable AI-use rules, not to keep trying detectors until one gives the answer you want.

## What an AI score actually tells you First distinguish an AI-writing indicator from a plagiarism or similarity report. One estimates patterns associated with generated text; the other identifies overlap with material in a database. Neither, on its own, establishes why the overlap or pattern occurred. [Turnitin's report guidance](https://guides.turnitin.com/hc/en-us/articles/22774058814093-Using-the-AI-Writing-Report) says its AI indicator should not be the sole basis for adverse action against a student. The percentage covers qualifying text only — prose sentences in a long-form writing format that the model judges could be AI-generated, including AI text later run through a paraphraser or bypasser tool. That is not every word in your file, and a high score does not tell you what assistance the institution permitted. ## The statistical trap: false positives are not a personal verdict Turnitin's [FAQ](https://www.turnitin.com/products/features/ai-writing-detection/faq) reports a document-level false-positive rate below 1% at the above-20% reporting threshold. That measures how often fully human documents are incorrectly flagged under its evaluation conditions. It does not mean a flagged document has less than a 1% chance of being human-written. Here is a deliberately simplified example, not a Turnitin test. Suppose 1,000 documents contain 900 human documents and 100 AI documents. An imaginary detector flags 1% of human documents and catches 80% of AI documents. It flags 9 human and 80 AI documents: 9 of 89 flags, about 10.1%, are wrong. The error rate among human documents and the error rate among flagged documents answer different questions. Changing the share of AI documents changes the second answer. Turnitin also published an approximately 4% false-positive figure for sentences in [June 2023](https://www.turnitin.com/blog/understanding-the-false-positive-rate-for-sentences-of-our-ai-writing-detection-capability). Treat that as a dated vendor claim, not a universal probability for any highlighted sentence today. Its [model release notes](https://guides.turnitin.com/hc/en-us/articles/28294949544717-AI-writing-detection-model) document subsequent updates. Document-level and sentence-level numbers are not interchangeable, and Turnitin has said that sentence-level accuracy is lower than document-level accuracy. One more wrinkle worth knowing before you argue about a number: after finding a higher-than-expected false-positive rate on documents under 20% AI writing, Turnitin replaced those low scores with an asterisk rather than a figure. ## If your essay or client draft gets flagged 1. **Keep the original file.** Save the submitted version, date, assignment or brief, and the report if you can access it. Do not overwrite the disputed document. 2. **Collect genuine process evidence.** Export available version history, outlines, notes and source links. Keep existing AI conversations if permitted and relevant. These are supporting context, not automatic proof. Do not fabricate drafts after the event. 3. **Read the rule that applied when you wrote it.** Check the course handbook, client agreement or employer policy. Grammar assistance, brainstorming and AI-generated paragraphs may be treated differently. 4. **Ask for a specific review.** Request the flagged passages, the tool and report date, and the rule allegedly breached. Ask how a human review or appeal works. 5. **Explain the process honestly.** Describe how you developed the argument and checked references. If you used AI, explain what it did. A clean detector result would not excuse undisclosed use that violated an agreed rule. Do not upload confidential client material or an unpublished assignment to a pile of free detector sites just to compare scores. Check the service's retention and privacy terms and whether you have permission to share the text. ### A neutral review request > Please share the passages that triggered the AI-writing concern and the policy applied to my submission. I can provide my existing notes and available document history, and explain my research and drafting process. Could you confirm the human-review and appeal procedure before a decision is made? Adapt that wording to your situation. It deliberately avoids claiming that version history conclusively proves authorship. ## For teachers and managers: use a review checklist - Separate the automated indicator from the final decision. - Compare the concern with the actual assignment or workplace rules. - Check whether the input meets the tool's requirements. Turnitin requires a file under 100 MB with at least 300 words of prose text in a long-form writing format, and no more than 30,000 words. Code, tables and bullet lists are not assessed the same way as essay prose. - Give the author a chance to explain the work and sources. - Record the reasons for the decision rather than copying a detector percentage into a verdict. In the US and UK, the relevant starting point is the particular school's, university's or employer's published procedure. The feature also has to be licensed and switched on by the institution, and administrators can turn it off — so do not assume every institution runs it, uses the same threshold, or treats a score as a legal conclusion. For an important disciplinary dispute, consult the appropriate student support service, union representative or qualified adviser. ## Why asking ChatGPT is not an authorship check [OpenAI's educator guidance](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/8313351-how-can-educators-respond-to-students-presenting-ai-generated-content-as-their-own) says its own research did not find detectors reliable enough, and it does not comment on other vendors' utility. It also warns that ChatGPT can invent answers to questions such as whether it wrote a passage. A chatbot's confident reply is not an audit trail. ## Watermarks solve a different, narrower problem Google's [SynthID Text documentation](https://ai.google.dev/responsible/docs/safeguards/synthid) describes a watermark inserted during generation by biasing token selection. Detection is still probabilistic, with watermarked, not-watermarked and uncertain outcomes. It is not a universal yes/no authorship test, and low-entropy output such as lists, code or plain facts carries a weaker signal, while short passages may fall below the length needed for a confident read. A positive result for supported content can help establish provenance. A missing watermark does not prove human authorship: the content may come from another system or have been changed. Google's [SynthID overview](https://deepmind.google/models/synthid/) identifies text from the Gemini app and web experience among its supported uses. Coverage and verification routes are not identical, either — the in-app SynthID check in Gemini, as of October 2026, covers images, video and audio, with roughly 10 checks of each type per rolling 24 hours, so do not assume you can paste a disputed essay somewhere and get a verdict. ## The useful replacement for a detector contest Before the next assignment or client project, agree on allowed assistance and what must be disclosed. Keep lightweight process records while working. A freelancer can retain the brief, an outline, source notes and the final fact-check checklist. A student can keep research notes and ordinary document history. That costs less effort than defending finished prose with competing opaque scores. *Updated October 2026. This guide is based on published vendor and platform documentation. No detector was tested for it, the worked example is hypothetical, and none of this is legal advice.* ## My Take I think the single most damaging habit in this whole area is treating a percentage as a measurement of a person. It isn't. It is an estimate about text, produced by a model whose own vendor says it should not be the sole basis for a decision, and the people most likely to be harmed by that confusion are the ones with the least power in the room. My read is that the 300-word minimum and the asterisk below 20% tell you more about the tool's limits than any accuracy headline does. A vendor that hides its own low scores because they misfire has already told you those scores are not evidence. If a score under 20% is too unreliable to display, it is too unreliable to open a misconduct case with. If you are a student or freelancer, the practical move is boring and it works: write in a tool that keeps version history, keep your notes, and ask for the specific passages and the specific rule before you say anything else. If you are the one reviewing, write down a reason that would still make sense if the detector number were deleted from the file. If you can't, you don't have a case yet. The fair point on the other side: detectors are not useless. On long, unedited model output submitted as original work, they catch real things, and an instructor with hundreds of papers needs some triage signal. I'd rather have a flawed starting point than pretend the problem doesn't exist. I'm not a lawyer or an academic-integrity officer, and nothing here is legal advice — for a disciplinary case with real consequences, get a student advocate, union rep or qualified adviser involved early. What I'd watch is institutions quietly turning the feature off rather than defending it, because that decision, more than any vendor statistic, is the honest verdict on how much weight these scores can carry.
